children: The stock of Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles (TMPV) fell 8.7 per cent last Monday, reacting to weak Q2 FY27 results. The stock ended the week with losses of 7.3 per cent. The underperformance is not limited to last week, and the stock has been weak for a while now. It is down 63 per cent from its all-time high of ₹714, hit in late-July 2024, and down about 33 per cent since we last wrote on it in October 2025, following the demerger of the commercial vehicles business. This is in contrast to other listed PV OEMs such as Maruti Suzuki, Hyundai and Mahindra & Mahindra, who have recorded fresh all-time highs in the second half of FY26 — an effect of the Street cheering growth prospects by virtue of GST rationalisation.

While the domestic Tata brand (Tata PVs) has done reasonably well, the underperformance has more to do with JLR (Jaguar Land Rover). JLR has had to navigate a tough FY26, following a cyber attack in September 2025, that halted production. Though business recovered in Q4 FY26, in H1 FY27, the brand had to contend with intense competition from local OEMs in the Chinese market. China accounted for 11-12 per cent of JLR’s volume in FY25-26. Further, there have been minor supply disruptions due to a fire at a component supplier’s facility and weakness in MENA (Middle East North Africa) market (6-7 per cent of volume in FY25-26) due to the Gulf conflict.

That said, JLR is about to begin deliveries of its new BEVs (battery electric vehicles) namely, the Range Rover, Range Rover Sport, Range Rover GT and Jaguar Type 01 from early 2027. Initiatives to bring about cost efficiencies are also underway. However, execution risks and competitive threats remain, infusing uncertainty for investors.

With this in mind, our SOTP (sum of the parts) price of TMPV ascribes a 1.5x-multiple to a conservative estimate of JLR’s FY28 EBITDA. This multiple is found towards the lower end of the range used by sell-side research and factors in the low growth potential, given JLR operates in the niche, luxury segment. For Tata PV business, we ascribe a 10x multiple to a conservative estimate of FY28 EBITDA. This is at a discount of about 50 per cent to the EV/EBITDA multiples of peers Maruti Suzuki and Hyundai, who have EBITDA margins close to 10 per cent, while Tata PV’s is lower at around 4 per cent. There is no meaningful upside at this SOTP price, making it unattractive to take fresh positions. Long-term investors who already hold the stock may continue to do so.
Here, we look at how TMPV has performed since we last wrote on the stock and explore its outlook.
We begin with JLR, which accounts for about 80 per cent of TMPV’s revenue.

After volume, revenue and PBT (bei) (profit before tax before exceptional items) grew -0.1 per cent,  3.8 per cent and 19.4 per cent respectively in FY25, JLR had a turbulent FY26. The three metrics fell 23.2 per cent, 13 per cent and 99 per cent respectively. FY26 volume fell  from 4,00,900 units in FY25 to 3,07,900 units.

A cyber incident in September to early-October 2025 chiefly explains this outcome. Systems had to be shut down, and the company had to give up on about a month’s production. This apart, demand weakness due to tariffs in the US, a 10-per cent luxury tax in China, now applicable on vehicles costing RMB 900,000 (~$135,000) from the earlier threshold of RMB 1,300,000 (~$195,000) and the planned wind-down of the existing Jaguar models (before the brand’s rebirth) are other factors that contributed to the slowdown.

Consequently, the company lost operating leverage. EBIT margin fell from 8.5 per cent in FY25 to 4.1 per cent in Q1, -8.7 per cent in Q2 and to -6.8 per cent in Q3, before recovering to 9.1 per cent in Q4. Though Tata PVs did well, TMPV slipped into losses (from continuing operations)  of ₹1,377 crore in FY26 from profit of ₹19,394 crore in FY25. Exceptional items worth ₹4,142 crore, including due to the cyber incident and voluntary separation package for employees, also weighed on earnings.

Moving on to FY27, in H1, volume and revenue grew 5.4 per cent and 13.2 per cent respectively. Do note that this is on a low base in H1 FY26 due to the cyber incident. Volume and revenue have grown at CAGRs of 11 per cent and 19 per cent over FY22-25, for context. Chinese competition — both in China and in the UK and Europe, weakness in MENA, continued wind-down of existing Jaguars along with a fire at a supplier’s facility explain the weaker business growth.

Higher marketing costs, higher share of low-margin ‘Discovery’ sales (production ends in December 2026) and rerouting of sales from weaker but high-margin Chinese and MENA markets to others such as the UK meant EBIT margin dropped to 2 per cent. PBT (bei) came in at ₹1,503 crore from -₹1,771 crore in H1 FY26. However, TMPV slipped into net losses (from continuing operations) of ₹4,592 crore, weighed down by exceptional items of ₹6,770 crore, including voluntary separation and impairment costs on investments.

Growth for Tata PV has been relatively better, driven by GST rationalisation. Volume grew 15.3 per cent in FY26 (14.3 per cent CAGR over FY22-25) and 42.6 per cent in H1 FY27. Revenue was up 21.7 per cent in FY26 (15.4 per cent CAGR over FY22-25) and 58.9 per cent in H1 FY27. Industry market share is up from 11.4 per cent in FY22, 13.2 per cent in FY25 to 14.3 per cent in H1 FY27. Traction for BEVs is robust, with BEVs accounting for 24 per cent of Tata PV sales versus 8 per cent for the industry in Q2 FY27.

Profitability of 1.4 per cent EBIT margin in FY26 was higher than FY25’s 0.9 per cent. However, due to extreme inflation in copper, rubber and steel due to the West Asia conflict, EBIT margin for H1 FY27 was -0.4 per cent. This is after 40 per cent of such inflation was absorbed through a cumulative price hike of 1.7 per cent in H1 FY27.

Looking ahead, here are the drivers for earnings growth. Deliveries of the new JLR BEVs start from 2027. These apart, Defender BEV is also set to be launched, but later. BEVs generally have higher selling price than ICE vehicles. JLR expects these to come in handy in its aim to deliver 10 per cent revenue growth consistently. A bunch of initiatives to drive efficiencies worth  £1.7 billion over FY27-28 at JLR is also underway (FY25 EBIT was around  £2.5 billion, for context).

These include reduction in the cost of sales, warranty cost and personnel cost (voluntary separation of about 4,000 employees). These are expected to bring breakeven volume down to three lakh  units. EBIT margin for FY27 is guided at 2-3 per cent and EBITDA margin for FY28 at double digits. Cost efficiency drives are also underway at Tata PVs to offset the end of EV PLI benefits (in 2028) and price hikes planned in Q3 and Q4 could shore margin.

Nevertheless, here are some risks to be mindful of. Chinese competition is real. Local OEMs now account for 70 per cent of Chinese PV market up from 41 per cent in 2021. Chinese exports also find their way into Europe and the UK. This, coupled with a potential negative wealth effect from an AI-related stock market correction, could dampen growth. Investors should also expect tapering growth for Tata PVs, on a high base set in FY26-27.

title: What should investors do about the stock of Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles?
